what: RxJS models things that happen over time (typing, clicks, HTTP responses, sockets) as streams you can combine, cancel and retry. NgRx builds on it: the Store keeps shared state with actions and reducers, and SignalStore is a lighter, signal-based way to hold feature state.
like: Like a conveyor belt of parcels with rules at each station: drop the old parcel when a new one arrives, or queue them, or ignore new ones while one is being handled.
why: Race conditions like stale search results are solved by one operator choice
Shared state gets one predictable path, with time-travel debugging in dev tools
Retries, debounce and cancellation are built in instead of hand-written

steps.d: A user action or socket message is an observable value pushed over time.
Operators like debounceTime tame noisy input before any request is made.

switchMap cancels the previous inner request when a new value arrives (good for reads). concatMap queues, mergeMap runs in parallel, exhaustMap ignores new values while one is running (good for a pay button).

steps.t: Run side effects in one place
steps.d: With the NgRx Store, Effects listen for actions, call APIs and dispatch result actions, keeping components free of request code.
The Store updates through reducers; SignalStore holds feature state as signals with methods that patch it.
Components read selectors or store signals and stay simple.

numbers.l: inner observable exhaustMap allows at a time; new projections are ignored until it completes
NgRx learning paths in the docs: Global Store and SignalStore
current NgRx docs version at time of writing

choices.d: Reads (search, route data): switchMap, so stale responses are cancelled. Writes that must all happen in order: concatMap. Independent parallel work: mergeMap. Double-click protection such as login or pay: exhaustMap.
Store (actions, reducers, effects, selectors) suits large teams, app-wide shared state and strict traceability. SignalStore suits feature or component state with less boilerplate.

choices.t: Signals or RxJS inside a component
choices.d: Use signals for the current value and RxJS where you need time operators, then bridge with toSignal.
Prefer the async pipe, toSignal or takeUntilDestroyed over manual subscribe to avoid leaks.

instead.why: When you only need current state and derived values
When most of the state is just cached server data

breaks.t: Wrong flattening operator on a payment
breaks.d: mergeMap or switchMap on a pay button lets a double tap send two requests, or cancel the first on the client while the server still charges.
breaks.see: Duplicate charges or an unknown outcome
breaks.fix: exhaustMap on the click, plus an idempotency key on the request

breaks.d: mergeMap on typeahead lets a slow old response overwrite a newer one.
breaks.see: Results flicker to an older query

say: For reads like search I use debounceTime then switchMap so a newer query cancels the older one.
For writes I choose by intent: concatMap when order matters, exhaustMap for a pay button, with an idempotency key on the server call.
I use the NgRx Store when many features share state and I want traceability, and SignalStore for feature-level state with less ceremony.

followups.q: Does switchMap cancel the server work?
followups.a: It unsubscribes on the client, which aborts the HTTP request, but the server may still have processed it. That is why writes use idempotency keys and not switchMap.

followups.q: When would you not use NgRx at all?
followups.a: For small apps or purely local state, signals and services are enough; add the Store when state is shared widely and needs tracing.

today: NgRx now documents two first-class paths, the global Store and SignalStore, so modern Angular teams often keep Store for app-wide state and use SignalStore for features, with signals as the read model.

check.q: Which NgRx option fits small feature-level state with little boilerplate?
check.why: SignalStore is the signal-based option designed for feature state.
